title: 2  Installing R
text:
2.1 Installing RStudio
Installing R and RStudio
R is the programming language software that will run the code we want to execute. RStudio is a separate piece of software called an Integrated Development Environment (IDE), which basically acts as a wrapper for R, and allows us to run our code while also providing lots of additional helpful features.
You could run your code directly in R if you wanted to, but most people will use of the many different IDEs thare are compataible with R (e.g. VSCode, Positron). For this class we will be using R and RStudio, as it is relatively simple to set up and easy to use.
R is maintained by a core team of developers, and is hosted at the The Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). RStudio is developed by a company called Posit. We will need to download both pieces of software separately.
The first step is to download R from The Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) here: https://cran.r-project.org/.
Windows
Click ‘Download R for Windows’, then ‘base’, then ‘Download R-4.61 for Windows’ (when you do it, this will list the most recent version of R instead). This will download an R installer. Run this file to open the R installation wizard, which will walk you through the installation. You can just select the default options at each stage.
Mac
Click ‘Download R for macOS’, then select the package version for your machine ‘R-4.6.1-arm64.pkg’ (this will list the most recent version of R). Just like for windows, this will download an R installer. Run this file to start the R installation wizard, which will walk you through the installation. You can just select the default options at each stage.
The next step is to download the RStudio IDE desktop version from the Posit website here: https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/#rstudio-ide-oss-downloads
Select the correct download for your computer’s operating system (Windows/Mac/Linux). Once the download is complete, run the file to begin the installation wizard and follow the instructions. You can select the default options throughout.

title: 4  Rendering Quarto PDFs with Tinytex
text:
4.1 Rendering PDFs in Quarto
In order to create PDFs with quarto, we need to have a LaTeX installation on our computer. LaTeX is a type of programming language used for typesetting pdf documents. The easiest way to get this working for Quarto is by installing a peice of software called ‘Tinytex’, which is a lighweight version of LaTeX.
crumbs: 4  Rendering Quarto PDFs with Tinytex

title: 4  Rendering Quarto PDFs with Tinytex
section: 4.2 Method 1 - Install via the tinytex R package
text:
4.2 Method 1 - Install via the tinytex R package
Open Rstudio, and run the code below in the console to install the tinytex R package

install.packages("tinytex")

Once the package is installed, run this code in the console

tinytex::install_tinytex()

This will download tinytex and install it on your computer. Once the installation is complete, you should now be able to render pdf files in Quarto.

title: 4  Rendering Quarto PDFs with Tinytex
section: 4.3 Method 2 - Install tinytex via Terminal in RStudio
text:
4.3 Method 2 - Install tinytex via Terminal in RStudio
If you have any issues with the first method, an alternative way of installing tinytex is by using the terminal within RStudio.

Step 1
Open RStudio, and click the ‘Terminal’ tab in the console window.







Step 2
You should see a window that looks like this, with a flashing cursor (the filepath that is shown here will be different on your computer).







Step 3
Type ‘quarto install tinytex’ and press enter.







Step 4
Tinytex will then download and install to your computer. Once complete, you can now render pdf files in quarto.







Step 5
If the file renders correctly, it should look something like this.





We can now create pdf files with Quarto!
